title: Common Spanish Politeness Mistakes (and Fixes)
meta_description: Spanish politeness mistakes: greeting in shops, asking for things, perdón vs disculpe vs lo siento, kisses, buen provecho, goodbyes, with fixes and a quiz.
excerpt: Polite in English isn’t always polite in Spanish, and vice versa.

body_html:
Spanish politeness mistakes rarely come from bad grammar. They come from carrying English habits into Spanish-speaking cultures, where politeness works differently. English relies heavily on “please”, “could you possibly” and indirect phrasing; Spanish relies more on warmth, greetings and tone. A perfectly correct sentence can sound cold, and a direct request can sound perfectly friendly. Here are the politeness mistakes I see learners make most often, and how to fix them.

Key takeaways
  • Greet people when you enter shops, elevators and waiting rooms: Buenos días.
  • Direct requests are normal in Spanish if your tone is warm: ¿Me da un café?
  • Perdón, disculpe and lo siento are not interchangeable.
  • Saying goodbye properly matters as much as saying hello.
{{toc}}

Spanish politeness mistakes with greetings

In many Spanish-speaking countries, it is polite to greet everyone when you walk into a small shop, an elevator, a doctor’s waiting room or a bus: Buenos días, Buenas tardes, or simply Buenas. Walking in silently can seem rude. The Centro Virtual Cervantes includes greetings and leave-taking among the core social functions every learner should master. When you leave, add Hasta luego or Adiós, gracias.

Kisses and handshakes

In Spain, friends and new acquaintances usually greet with two kisses on the cheek (right cheek first). In most of Latin America, it’s one kiss. Men greeting men usually shake hands or hug. In business, a handshake is safe everywhere. Follow the lead of the person you are greeting.

Asking for things

Learners often think direct requests are rude, so they produce very long, indirect sentences that sound odd in Spanish. In a café in Mexico, ¿Me da un café? or simply Un café, por favor is perfectly polite, and in Colombia you’ll hear ¿Me regala…?. In Spain, bars are even more direct: ¿Me pones una caña? Use the conditional for more formal requests: ¿Podría ayudarme? See {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

What makes a request polite in Spanish is mostly tone, a greeting first and gracias after. In Spain, people say por favor less than learners say “please”, and that’s not rude.

{{image:2}}

Perdón, disculpe, lo siento, con permiso

PhraseUse it to…Example
Perdón / PerdonaApologize for a small thing; get attention¡Perdón! No te había visto.
Disculpe / DisculpaGet attention politely; apologizeDisculpe, ¿la estación?
Lo sientoExpress real regret or sympathyLo siento mucho por tu pérdida.
Con permisoPass someone or leave a roomCon permiso, voy a bajar.

Using lo siento to squeeze past someone sounds too heavy. More in {{link:how-to-apologize-in-spanish|how to apologize in Spanish}} and {{link:condolences-in-spanish|condolences in Spanish}}.

Getting a waiter’s attention

In Spain, ¡Perdona! or ¡Oiga! (formal) is normal. In Mexico, joven or señorita is common, and ¿Me trae la cuenta, por favor? works everywhere. Waving or clicking your fingers is rude almost everywhere. Also remember that in many countries the check is not brought until you ask for it; it’s considered rude to rush diners. See {{link:ordering-food-in-spanish|ordering food in Spanish}}.

{{book:love-slowly}}

At the table

  • Say ¡Buen provecho! or ¡Que aproveche! when others start eating, or when you pass people eating.
  • Compliment the food: ¡Qué rico está todo! See {{link:how-to-compliment-food-in-spanish|how to compliment food in Spanish}}.
  • Don’t rush away after the meal: the sobremesa, chatting at the table, is part of the meal.
  • Refusing food once is normal; your host may insist, and you can accept a little.

Saying no and saying goodbye

A bare No can sound abrupt. Soften it: No, gracias, Es que… (It’s just that…), Me encantaría, pero…. And when you leave a gathering, say goodbye to everyone, often individually. The so-called “Irish goodbye”, slipping out unnoticed, can seem quite rude in Spanish-speaking cultures.

Usted, tú and titles

Choosing tú with an older stranger, or usted with a young friend, can sound rude or distant. When in doubt, start with usted. See {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}. Titles like don and doña before first names show respect to older people: don Antonio, doña Carmen.

Common mistakes

MistakeBetter
Entering a shop in silence¡Buenos días!
Lo siento to get past someonePerdón / Con permiso
¿Qué? when you didn’t hear¿Perdón? / ¿Cómo?
Leaving without saying goodbyeBueno, me voy. ¡Hasta luego a todos!
Quiero un café. (can sound demanding)¿Me da un café? / Un café, por favor.
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. You walk into a bakery at 10 a.m. (¡Buenos días!)
  2. You need to get past someone on the bus. (Perdón, con permiso.)
  3. You didn’t hear what someone said. (¿Perdón? ¿Cómo?)
  4. Your hosts start eating. (¡Buen provecho!)
  5. You leave a party. (Bueno, me voy. Muchas gracias por todo.)

All mistake types in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish politeness is about warmth and presence more than formulas. Greet people, say goodbye, choose the right “sorry”, use a friendly tone with direct requests, and enjoy the meal. Get these right, and people will remember you as muy educado, very well-mannered.

faq.q: Is it rude not to say por favor in Spanish?
faq.a: Not necessarily. In Spain especially, direct requests like ¿Me pones un café? are polite with a friendly tone. Greetings and thanks matter more.

faq.q: What is the difference between perdón, disculpe and lo siento?
faq.a: Perdón and disculpe are for small apologies and getting attention. Lo siento expresses real regret or sympathy. Con permiso is for passing someone.

faq.q: Should I greet people when entering a shop in Spanish-speaking countries?
faq.a: Yes. A simple Buenos días or Buenas when you enter, and Hasta luego when you leave, is expected in many places.
